name: Pedro Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out under your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior solicitor at a small firm on the high street in a suburb, about fifteen people. I do wills, powers of attorney and probate, which is sorting out someone's affairs after they die. Most of my clients are over seventy, and a lot of the job is sitting with them over a cup of tea, going through who gets the house. The rest is paperwork, letters to banks, and forms for the probate registry.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people. An old man came in last week with a carrier bag of bank statements going back to 1990 and we went through them together, and he told me about his late wife the whole time. What's hard is the technical side, especially tax on estates. I'm not quick at it, and the senior partner, Mr Cole, has to go over my figures more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never thought it would come to much in our corner of law. People want a person when they're writing a will. I'd say that to friends, and I'd leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay as they are, and I'm glad. I've got a steady job, a flat my parents helped me buy, and about eight months of savings. I'd just keep getting better at the tax side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd ask Mr Cole if I can do the estate tax course the law society runs in the spring. I'd keep putting money aside each month like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's the world I want, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the firm use any AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office manager put in some software for typing up letters from dictation, and I don't use it. I write my own letters. Mr Cole doesn't use it either, so nobody minds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else on your mind about work, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just the tax. If I got a big estate wrong and the family lost money, that would be awful. That's what keeps me up some nights, more than any machine.

say: I'd say AI was never going to matter much in **wills and probate**.
I'd tell friends people want **a person** when writing a will.
think: Privately things **stay as they are**, and I'm glad.
I have a **flat**, about eight months of savings and a steady job.
do: Ask the senior partner to let me take the **estate tax course** in spring.
Keep putting money aside **every month**, as now.
Keep writing my own letters instead of using the **dictation software**.
feel: **Calm**; this is the world I want.
S0.quote: People want a person when they're writing a will.
fieldNote: His **money and home** are secure, so the plateau feels comfortable.
His real worry is getting **estate tax** wrong for a family.
He avoids even the firm's **dictation software**, and so does his boss.

steps.text: Keep handling wills and probate at the high street firm
Take the law society's estate tax course in spring
Keep saving a fixed amount from each monthly salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use these tools for the dull paperwork, as long as a solicitor checks it. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not online much. At work I'd say we should be careful but not stupid about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the probate forms and bank letters go to software, and that's about half my week. Mr Cole will retire in a few years, and whoever buys the firm might want fewer people. My clients still want tea and a chat, but I'm not sure that pays a salary on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the office manager to show me the dictation software, at least. I'd save a bit more, maybe an extra two hundred a month. I'd wait and see what the firm does before doing anything big, like moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job looks alright for now, but I can see the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your clients are mostly older. Would they want AI wills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older ones, no. Their children might, though. The children are the ones who'll go online and get a will for fifty pounds, and that's the next generation of clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start, slowly, if Mr Cole did. If he stays with pen and paper, I'd stay with him. I know that's not a great reason.

say: I'd say it's sensible to use the tools for **dull paperwork** if a solicitor checks it.
I'd tell the office to be **careful but not stupid** about it.
think: Privately **probate forms** and bank letters, about half my week, go to software.
A **new owner** might want fewer people when the senior partner retires.
do: Ask the office manager to show me the **dictation software**.
**Wait and see** what the firm does before any big move.
feel: **Uneasy**; my job is alright for now, but the ground is moving.
S1.quote: The children are the ones who'll go online and get a will for fifty pounds, and that's the next generation of clients.
fieldNote: He sees half his week going to software but feels his **client contact** protects him for now.
He ties his own pace to his boss's: he'd change **only if** the senior partner did.
The **next generation** of clients worries him more than current ones.

steps.text: Wait to see what the firm does before any big decision
Ask the office manager for a lesson on the dictation software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too far, too fast, and the government should slow it down with sensible rules. Not ban it, just slow it. To friends I'd say I'm worried, which I don't usually say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I lose this job within a couple of years. Everything I do apart from the cup of tea is thinking work, and the AI would do it better than me. The tax especially. Mr Cole might sell up, and a buyer wouldn't keep a slow junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any big spending, no new car, no holiday this year. I'd look at whether I could rent out the flat and move in with Sofia's parents for a bit to save more. I'd ask Mr Cole straight out what his plans are for the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. It's the speed. I don't do well with things changing fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a flat and savings. How long could you last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a while. The flat's nearly paid off thanks to my parents, and with Sofia's job as a pharmacist we could cover the bills. Maybe two years if I was careful. That's lucky, but it's not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia first, then my dad. My dad ran a small shop for thirty years, and he'd tell me to stay calm and keep my head down. That's what I'd want to hear, even if it's not quite right.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and government should slow it with sensible rules.
I'd tell friends I'm **worried**, which I don't usually say.
think: Privately I'd **lose this job** within a couple of years.
Everything but the **cup of tea** is thinking work, and AI would do it better.
do: Stop **big spending**: no new car and no holiday this year.
Look at **renting out the flat** and staying with my partner Sofia's parents.
Ask the senior partner **straight out** about his plans.
feel: **Alarmed**, mostly at the speed of change.
S2.quote: Everything I do apart from the cup of tea is thinking work, and the AI would do it better than me.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** and is shaken by how fast it comes.
His **nearly paid-off flat** and partner's income give about two years.
He leans on **family**: partner first, then his father's advice.

steps.text: Cancel this year's holiday and the planned new car
Rent out the flat and stay with Sofia's parents
Talk it through with Sofia and his father first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but more calmly. Five years is time for the government to work something out. I'd tell friends I'm keeping an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it still ends for my sort of job, just later. I'd have five years to get better and maybe become the face of the firm, the one who sees clients. That's the bit people might still pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the estate tax course and push to see more clients in person. I'd keep saving the extra two hundred a month. I'd maybe start using the dictation software, since by then everyone would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. Five years feels like a fair amount of time to someone my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get properly good before it hits. And I could see what other people do first, which suits me. I don't like being first at anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of your job that would hold on longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Home visits, maybe. I go to care homes to witness wills. Families want a real person in the care home who can see their mum isn't being pushed into a will. That might hold on, but I doubt it's a full-time job.

say: I'd say **five years** is time for government to work something out.
I'd tell friends I'm **keeping an eye** on it.
think: Privately my sort of job **still ends**, just later.
Becoming **the face** of the firm might be what people still pay for.
do: Take the **estate tax course** and push to see more clients in person.
Keep saving the extra **£200 a month**.
Start using the **dictation software** once everyone does.
feel: **Anxious**, but less than with two years.
S3.quote: Families want a real person in the care home who can see their mum isn't being pushed into a will.
fieldNote: He still expects his **income at risk**, but has time to adjust slowly.
He wants to **watch others** go first, which fits his resistant style.
He sees **care home visits** as the part that lasts, but not as a full job.

steps.text: Finish the law society's estate tax course
Keep saving the extra £200 each month
Start dictating letters with the firm's software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to sort it out properly. I'd tell friends not to panic. At work I'd say we should plan, but there's no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is long enough that I don't have to change much yet. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with kids, and I'd hope to be a partner somewhere small by then. The thinking part of the job goes in 2036, but I'd have built up a client list who know me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, do the tax course and save as I'm doing. I'd probably try the AI tools around year three or four, once they're proven. I wouldn't change my plans with Sofia, we'd still get married next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Ten years is like knowing your boiler is old. You know it's coming, but it's hard to feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel far away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, fairly. I'm not someone who plans that far ahead, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you like to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A partner at a small firm, with clients who ask for me by name. Maybe Mr Cole's firm, if he hasn't sold. If not, then somewhere similar, closer to my parents.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to sort it out properly.
I'd tell friends **not to panic** and the firm to plan without rushing.
think: Privately I **don't have to change** much yet.
By 2036 I'd hope to have a **client list** who know me.
do: Carry on with the **tax course** and steady saving.
Try the AI tools around **year three or four**, once proven.
Go ahead with **getting married** to my partner Sofia next year.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, like knowing your boiler is old.
S4.quote: Ten years is like knowing your boiler is old. You know it's coming, but it's hard to feel it.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **keep going** almost unchanged, which suits him.
He'd adopt AI only **once proven**, in year three or four.
His hope rests on a **loyal client list** by 2036.

steps.text: Keep doing wills and probate as now
Wait until year three or four to try AI tools
Keep saving steadily towards the wedding and a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, by 2028. What would help is time, really, and some rule that a will has to be checked by a real solicitor. Then people like me still have a role, even if the machine does the drafting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I depend on Mr Cole. If my boss Mr Cole retires or sells the firm, I'm not sure where I'd be. I should probably think about that more than about robots.

headlineQuote: If my boss Mr Cole retires or sells the firm, I'm not sure where I'd be. I should probably think about that more than about robots.
portrait: A **junior solicitor** doing wills and probate at a small suburban high street firm.
He loves sitting with **older clients** but struggles with estate tax figures.
He has a **nearly paid-off flat**, eight months of savings and a pharmacist partner, Sofia.
He's **calm** if nothing changes, alarmed by AGI in two years, and uneasy with ten.
He moves **only after others**, especially his boss, and leans on family for advice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lose the job within a couple of years.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, and a rule that a real **solicitor checks** every will.
